intro: Requests Meridian is likely to make. Each one leaves the blueprint. Decide each card and watch what the project carries.
punchline: This is how a client ends up with a system designed for them instead of to best practice.

riskLevels.label: On blueprint
riskLevels.description: Standard process. Upgrades and testing stay routine.

riskLevels.label: Contained
riskLevels.description: A few deliberate exceptions, each with an owner.

riskLevels.label: Elevated
riskLevels.description: Exceptions start to shape the design and the test plan.

riskLevels.label: High
riskLevels.description: Every release now needs regression work on custom code.

riskLevels.label: Severe
riskLevels.description: The system is designed around legacy habit. Upgrades become projects.

requests.request: Pull every request from our external portal and inbox automatically on day one.
requests.context: Branches re-key requests today and want the typing gone immediately.
requests.blueprintAlternative: Go live with manual intake into one queue. Integrate each channel once the required intake fields have held steady for a few weeks.
requests.ongoingDetail: Every channel becomes an interface to monitor, and field changes on either side break it.
askWhy: Which channel carries most of the volume today?
Are the intake fields settled enough to map yet?
What does re-keying cost per request, measured, not guessed?

requests.request: Keep our shop system for technician work and sync it both ways.
requests.context: Technicians know the shop system, and some reports depend on it.
requests.blueprintAlternative: Choose one system of record for the technician's job. Draw a clear boundary and send data one way.
requests.ongoingDetail: Two systems of record for the same job, with sync conflicts to resolve every week.
askWhy: Which activities truly need the shop system?
When the two disagree about a job, which one wins?
Is the concern the tool itself, or the history inside it?

requests.request: Technicians should only see jobs in their own territory.
requests.context: Branch managers want control over their own people.
requests.blueprintAlternative: Use territory as a scheduling preference. Dispatch can cross a boundary to cover staffing gaps, and every cross-territory job is visible.
requests.ongoingDetail: Custom scheduling rules have to be retested whenever territories or staffing change.
askWhy: How often does a job cross territories today?
Who covers a territory when its technician is out?
Is the goal control, or visibility of who is working where?

requests.request: Let technicians change prices and costs on the job.
requests.context: The price list is often wrong, so technicians fix prices on site.
requests.blueprintAlternative: Price from the price list. Technicians flag exceptions for approval, and the price list gets fixed where it is wrong.
requests.ongoingDetail: Cheap to allow, expensive to carry: margin varies by who shows up, and nobody can audit why.
askWhy: Which prices are wrong most often?
Would an approval step on exceptions be fast enough on site?
Who owns keeping the price list right?

requests.request: Automate every customer's mileage and travel-charge rules at go-live.
requests.context: Many customers have their own flat rates and mileage thresholds.
requests.blueprintAlternative: Start with standard travel charges on the price list. Automate the few highest-volume customer rules in phase two.
requests.ongoingDetail: Every customer rule becomes custom logic to retest whenever prices or contracts change.
askWhy: How many customers have a travel rule that is actually different?
How much revenue do those rules represent?
Could the unusual cases be priced by hand for now?

requests.request: Keep our truck-based work order numbers.
requests.context: Reports and customer conversations use the old numbering.
requests.blueprintAlternative: Use the system's work order number, and store the truck or business unit as a reportable field.
requests.ongoingDetail: Custom numbering has to survive every upgrade and every integration that creates work orders.
askWhy: Who reads the number, and what do they learn from it?
Would a truck field on the work order answer the same question?
Do customers ever quote the number back to you?
